notes.b: Every living thing needs nitrogen, yet the huge store in the air is out of reach for almost all of them. Nitrogen therefore has to be converted into usable forms and then recycled, or life would run out of it.
points: Living things need nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins, nucleic acids (DNA and RNA), ATP (the cell's energy carrier) and chlorophyll (the green pigment in plants). Minerals goes into why plants need it and the signs of deficiency.
About 78% of the air is nitrogen gas (N₂), but plants and animals cannot use it. The two atoms are held together by a very strong triple bond that few organisms can break.

Plants can absorb nitrogen only as ions dissolved in soil water, mainly nitrate (NO₃⁻) and also ammonium (NH₄⁺). So nitrogen must be converted, or fixed, before it enters food chains, and recycled from dead matter.

The forms to recognise are nitrogen gas (N₂); ammonia (NH₃) and ammonium (NH₄⁺); nitrite (NO₂⁻); nitrate (NO₃⁻); and organic nitrogen, which is nitrogen built into proteins, nucleic acids and urea (the waste molecule in mammals' urine).
notes.tip: Exams ask the form in which plants absorb nitrogen: nitrate (and ammonium), never nitrogen gas. Plants cannot take N₂ from the air, even legumes.

notes.b: Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds that living things can use, such as ammonium, ammonia or nitrate. The biological route is carried out by bacteria, either living freely or in partnership with plants.
points: Free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in water convert N₂ to ammonium, which they use to make their own proteins. When they die, decomposition releases the nitrogen to the soil.
Other nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in root nodules (small swellings on the roots) of legumes, the pea family, for example clover, peas and beans. They fix nitrogen for the plant.

The bacteria give the plant ammonium, which it uses to make amino acids. The plant gives the bacteria carbohydrates from photosynthesis and a protected, low-oxygen home. Both benefit, so this is mutualism.

Fixation takes a lot of energy, supplied as ATP from the bacteria's respiration, and uses an enzyme that oxygen damages. This is why nodules keep oxygen levels low: they contain a red pigment that binds oxygen, so active nodules are pink inside.
Legumes grow well in nitrogen-poor soil because their bacteria supply the nitrogen. When they die or are ploughed in, the nitrogen in their tissues enriches the soil.
Clover grown with grass, and legumes in crop rotation (growing different crops in turn on the same field), reduce the need for nitrogen fertiliser. This is why farmers grow clover.
notes.tip: If asked about root nodules, say the bacteria fix nitrogen into ammonium for the plant and the plant supplies carbohydrates and a low-oxygen home. Do not say the plant fixes nitrogen itself. Do not call nitrification 'fixation'.

notes.h: Nitrogen fixation by lightning and industry
notes.b: Bacteria are not the only route from nitrogen gas to usable nitrogen. Lightning does a little of it naturally, and humans do a great deal of it in factories.
points: Atmospheric fixation by lightning: the energy of lightning makes nitrogen react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides, which dissolve in rain and reach the soil as nitrate. This is a small contribution compared with biological fixation.
Industrial fixation by the Haber process: nitrogen from the air combines with hydrogen (made mainly from natural gas) at high temperature and pressure to make ammonia.
The ammonia is turned into nitrogen fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate and urea, which farmers spread to give crops usable nitrogen.
Human activity, mainly the Haber process, now fixes at least as much nitrogen each year as all natural processes on land. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.

notes.h: Assimilation and passing along food chains
notes.b: Once nitrogen is in the soil as nitrate or ammonium, it moves into living things and along food chains. Assimilation means the plant builds absorbed nitrogen into its own molecules.
points: Uptake: plant roots absorb nitrate and ammonium from soil water. Nitrate is taken in by active transport, against its concentration gradient, using ATP, and travels to the leaves in the xylem (the tubes that carry water up the plant).
Assimilation: the plant uses the nitrogen, together with sugars from photosynthesis, to make amino acids, then proteins, and also nucleic acids and chlorophyll.
Feeding: animals get nitrogen only by eating plants or other animals. They digest the proteins into amino acids and build their own proteins from them.
Excretion and death: animals excrete excess nitrogen (in mammals, as urea in urine). Faeces, urine, dead plants and dead animals return organic nitrogen to the soil.

notes.b: Dead matter and wastes are full of organic nitrogen that plants cannot use directly. Decomposition is the step that turns it back into a usable form.
points: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on dead organisms, faeces and urine. They digest the proteins and other nitrogen compounds and release the nitrogen as ammonia, which dissolves in soil water as ammonium (NH₄⁺). This step is often called ammonification (putrefaction).
Without decomposition, the nitrogen in dead matter would be locked up and the soil would run out of usable nitrogen.
Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, aerated soil (soil with air spaces), because these conditions suit the decomposers. There is more on this in The carbon cycle.
Ammonium is the starting point for nitrification. Some ammonium is also taken up directly by plants.
notes.tip: Decomposition produces ammonium, not nitrate directly. Nitrate only appears after the next step, nitrification.

notes.b: Ammonium from decomposition is not the form plants take up most. Nitrifying bacteria in the soil convert it to nitrate in two steps.
points: Nitrification is the conversion of ammonium into nitrate by nitrifying bacteria in the soil, in two steps. First, one group of nitrifying bacteria oxidises ammonium (NH₄⁺) to nitrite (NO₂⁻). Second, a second group oxidises nitrite to nitrate (NO₃⁻).

Nitrifying bacteria are aerobic: they need oxygen. Nitrification is therefore fastest in well-drained, well-aerated soil. Ploughing and draining help it, while waterlogging (soil with all its air spaces filled with water) stops it.
Nitrifying bacteria are autotrophic (they make their own food): they get energy from these chemical reactions (chemosynthesis) rather than from light or from eating other organisms.

Nitrate is the form plants absorb most. It is also very soluble and is not held by soil particles, so heavy rain easily washes it out of the soil (leaching) into ground water, rivers and lakes. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
notes.tip: Exams ask why ploughing increases soil nitrate: it aerates the soil, so aerobic nitrifying bacteria can make nitrate. Nitrification needs oxygen, while denitrification does not, and students often swap them.

notes.b: Nitrification builds up nitrate in the soil. Denitrification is the opposite journey, returning nitrogen to the air and completing the cycle.
points: Denitrification is the conversion of nitrate in the soil back into nitrogen gas (N₂) by denitrifying bacteria. This returns nitrogen to the atmosphere and completes the cycle.

Denitrifying bacteria work in anaerobic conditions (no oxygen), such as waterlogged, compacted or poorly drained soils and the mud of lakes and marshes. They use nitrate in place of oxygen in respiration.
Denitrification removes usable nitrogen from the soil, lowering fertility, so farmers drain wet land to stop it.
It also gives off some nitrous oxide (N₂O), a greenhouse gas (one that traps heat in the atmosphere). There is more on this in Climate change and biological strategies.
In wetlands and water treatment, denitrification is useful because it removes excess nitrate before it reaches rivers.
notes.tip: Exams ask why waterlogged soils are low in nitrate: no oxygen, so nitrification stops and denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into N₂. Denitrification happens without oxygen, the reverse of nitrification.

notes.b: Fixation, decomposition, nitrification and denitrification are the four named processes of the cycle. Comparing them side by side shows what each converts, who does it, and what it needs.
points: Fixation: N₂ becomes ammonium. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (free-living or in nodules) do it. It is anaerobic inside a nodule, and it adds usable nitrogen.
Decomposition: organic nitrogen becomes ammonium. Bacteria and fungi do it. It is aerobic or anaerobic, and it recycles nitrogen.
Nitrification: ammonium becomes nitrite and then nitrate. Nitrifying bacteria do it. It needs oxygen, and it makes the form plants use most.
Denitrification: nitrate becomes N₂. Denitrifying bacteria do it. It needs no oxygen, and it removes usable nitrogen.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to define each of these four processes and to name the process at a given arrow in a diagram. Learn what each one converts, from and to.

notes.h: Using the model to predict, and its limitations
notes.b: A model is useful because it lets you work out what happens when conditions change. It also has limits, and exams may ask you to name them.
points: Prediction (a): if a field becomes waterlogged, nitrification stops and denitrification increases, so soil nitrate falls and plants become nitrogen-deficient.
Prediction (b): if a farmer grows clover, fixation increases, so there is more soil nitrogen the next season.
Prediction (c): heavy rain after fertiliser is spread leaches nitrate into a river. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.
Limitation: the model shows the processes but not their rates or amounts.
Limitation: it does not show where nitrogen is lost, such as by leaching or by ammonia escaping from slurry (liquid animal waste), unless these are added.
Limitation: real soils contain many more microorganisms and steps than the four named groups. There is more on general limitations of models in Models.
notes.tip: Exams ask why waterlogged soils are low in nitrate, and why farmers grow clover. Use the cause-and-effect chains in the predictions above.

notes.b: The nitrogen cycle is modelled as a labelled diagram: boxes for the stores of nitrogen and arrows for the processes that move nitrogen between them.
points: Arrows for the gains of usable nitrogen: fixation (air → nodules → plant; air → free-living bacteria → soil ammonium); lightning (air → nitrate); Haber process and fertiliser (air → soil nitrate).

Arrows for the movement and recycling of nitrogen: absorption (soil nitrate → plants); feeding (plants → animals); death and excretion (→ dead matter); decomposition (dead matter → ammonium); nitrification (ammonium → nitrite → nitrate); denitrification (nitrate → air).

Diagram: boxes for nitrogen gas in air; plants (proteins); animals (proteins); dead organisms and wastes (faeces, urine); soil ammonium; nitrite; soil nitrate; legume root nodules. Join them with the labelled arrows.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to draw or complete a labelled nitrogen-cycle diagram, so label every arrow with its process name.

keyTerms.definition: The conversion of nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds, such as ammonium, that living things can use.
A small swelling on the roots of a legume that contains nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
A member of the pea family, such as clover, peas or beans, whose root nodules fix nitrogen.
The release of nitrogen from dead organisms and wastes as ammonia, which dissolves as ammonium; also called decomposition in this cycle.
The two-step oxidation of ammonium to nitrite and then to nitrate by aerobic nitrifying bacteria.
The conversion of nitrate back into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria in anaerobic conditions.
The washing of soluble nitrate out of the soil into ground water, rivers and lakes by rain.
The industrial reaction of nitrogen from the air with hydrogen at high temperature and pressure to make ammonia.
A greenhouse gas, N₂O, released from soils by denitrification.

questions.model: Nitrification converts ammonium into nitrate in two steps: first ammonium is oxidised to nitrite, then nitrite is oxidised to nitrate, both by groups of nitrifying bacteria. It needs oxygen, so it is fastest in well-drained, well-aerated soil. Denitrification converts nitrate back into nitrogen gas, carried out by denitrifying bacteria. It happens in anaerobic conditions, such as waterlogged soil, where the bacteria use nitrate in place of oxygen in respiration. Nitrification makes nitrogen usable by plants, while denitrification removes it from the soil.

questions.prompt: Model the nitrogen cycle, with reference to nitrogen fixation, nitrification, decomposition and denitrification. Include a labelled diagram.
questions.model: A labelled diagram shows nitrogen gas in the air, nitrogen compounds in plants, animals, dead matter and the soil, root nodules of legumes, nitrite and nitrate, joined by arrows for fixation, absorption, feeding, excretion, decomposition, nitrification and denitrification. Nitrogen fixation converts N₂ into ammonium, carried out by free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria or by bacteria in root nodules. Decomposition, carried out by bacteria and fungi, releases nitrogen from dead organisms and wastes as ammonium. Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrite and then to nitrate, which is the form plants absorb most. Denitrification converts nitrate back into nitrogen gas in waterlogged, anaerobic soil. Plants take up nitrate and ammonium by active transport, use them to make amino acids and proteins, and animals gain nitrogen by eating them.

questions.prompt: A farmer's field becomes waterlogged for several weeks. Use the nitrogen cycle to predict and explain the effect on the crop, and suggest how growing clover could help the following year.
questions.model: Waterlogging makes the soil anaerobic. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification stops and no new nitrate is made from ammonium. Denitrifying bacteria work without oxygen, so they convert soil nitrate into nitrogen gas, which escapes to the air. Soil nitrate therefore falls, and plants that depend on nitrate become nitrogen-deficient, so the crop grows poorly. Clover is a legume with root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Growing it fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium that the plant uses, and when the clover dies or is ploughed in, its nitrogen enriches the soil for the following year's crop.
